en: To make something more noticeable or prominent; to emphasize
hook: ACCENTUATE: put an ACCENT on it to make it stand out.
story: Accentuate. To make something more noticeable or prominent; to emphasise. Before her cousin's wedding, Nell sat still while her aunt drew a thin line of eyeliner along her eyes. Nothing else changed, yet suddenly her eyes looked twice as large. "Eyeliner does not change your face," her aunt said. "It only accentuates what is already there." The yellow sari accentuated the glow of the turmeric too. To accentuate is to put an accent on something, the way a stressed syllable stands out in a word. So, what verb means to make a feature stand out more? ... Accentuate.

gre.s: The designer used dark frames and bright lighting to ____ the paintings' vivid colors, making them seem to glow against the gray walls.
gre.clue: making them seem to glow

example: Staining the sample with iodine accentuates the starch granules, making them easy to count under the microscope.

en: Someone who speaks up for a disputed belief, person, or policy
hook: GRE trick: an APOLOGIST doesn't apologize — he DEFENDS.
story: Apologist. Someone who speaks up for a disputed belief, person, or policy. At a tea stall in town, the men argued every evening about a new factory that was dirtying the river. Most were angry. But Seth, who worked at the factory, defended it each time, insisting it brought jobs and the river would recover. His friends called him the factory's apologist. Careful: an apologist does not apologise. The Greek apologia means a speech in defence, so an apologist defends. So, what do you call a person who keeps defending a controversial cause? ... Apologist.

gre.s: Even his most loyal ____ struggled to justify the general's brutal treatment of civilians.
gre.clue: struggled to justify

example: Even apologists for the old colonial railway admit that it was built mainly to carry jute and tea to the ports, not passengers.

en: To attribute something to a particular cause or source
hook: A-SCRIBE: the scribe writes down who caused it.
story: Ascribe. To attribute something to a particular cause or source. When Tucker came first in his class, his grandmother ascribed it to the fish head curry she had fed him every Friday. [chuckle] His teacher ascribed it to his late-night practice. Tucker himself ascribed it to both, and asked for another fish head. Scribe means to write, so to ascribe is to write a cause next to a result, like a label. So, what verb means to credit a result to a particular cause? ... Ascribe.

gre.s: Early scholars tended to ____ the epic to a single poet, but most now believe it was composed by many authors over several centuries.
gre.clue: composed by many authors over several centuries

example: Villagers once ascribed their district's high rate of goiter to bad luck, until researchers traced it to a lack of iodine in the diet.

en: Damaged or spoiled; suffering from decay
hook: BLIGHT: a plant disease that withers crops.
story: Blighted. Damaged or spoiled; suffering from decay. Ken grew up beside a clear canal in the old city, where children once swam on hot afternoons. Returning after twenty years abroad, he found it blighted: black water, plastic bags caught in the reeds, and a smell that made his eyes sting. He stood on the bridge for a long time in silence. Blight is a disease that withers crops, like the famous potato blight; a blighted place looks as if that disease has spread through it. So, what word describes a place spoiled and decaying? ... Blighted.

gre.s: Once a thriving industrial district, the riverside neighborhood is now ____, its factories abandoned and its streets lined with crumbling, boarded-up houses.
gre.clue: its factories abandoned and its streets lined with crumbling, boarded-up houses

example: Volunteers planted fruit trees across the blighted farmland, where saltwater from the cyclone had killed every crop the previous year.

en: To restrain or control; also, to show resentment or anger
bn: সংযত করা; লাগাম টানা, ক্ষোভ প্রকাশ করা
hook: BRIDLE: the straps on a horse's head that hold it back.
story: Bridle. As a noun, the straps that control a horse's head. As a verb, to restrain, or to bristle with resentment. When a guest at dinner suggested that Lisa, a doctor, should give up her job after marriage, Lisa felt herself bridle. Her cheeks went hot. But she bridled her temper, smiled, and said she had worked too hard to stop now. Picture a horse jerking its head back against the bridle: that is the angry bridling, and the straps holding it are the restraint. So, what verb means to bristle at an insult? ... Bridle.

gre.s: The coach urged his young striker to ____ his temper, since another red card would mean missing the final.
gre.clue: since another red card would mean missing the final

example: Learning to bridle his impatience, the young doctor began listening to each patient's whole story before reaching for a prescription pad.

en: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and unpredictably
hook: CAPRICIOUS sounds like a CAPRI goat: it jumps randomly from rock to rock.
story: Capricious. Changing mood or behaviour suddenly and unpredictably. Every fisherman on the coast knows the monsoon sea is capricious. One morning Jack's uncle set out under a clear blue sky; by noon, black clouds rolled in and the waves rose like walls. Two hours later, the sun was shining again as if nothing had happened. He came home soaked but safe, [sigh] and his family breathed again. Capricious sounds like Capricorn, the goat, which leaps from rock to rock without warning. So, what word describes weather or a person that changes suddenly, without reason? ... Capricious.

gre.s: Investors grew wary of the regulator, whose rulings seemed ____, reversing course from month to month without any stated rationale.
gre.clue: reversing course from month to month without any stated rationale

example: The landlord's capricious rules changed every month, banning guests one week and cooking with gas the next.

en: Intended to make peace and reduce anger
hook: CONCILIATORY: brings a peace COUNCIL together.
story: Conciliatory. Intended to make peace and reduce anger. Two city neighbours had not spoken for a month after an argument over a parking space. Then one evening, Molly's mother crossed the corridor with a bowl of warm rice pudding and said, "Let us not fight over a car." It was a conciliatory gesture, and the next morning the bowl came back full of cookies. A conciliatory word is often all a quarrel needs. Conciliatory is linked to council: it brings people back together to talk in peace. So, what word describes an action meant to calm a quarrel? ... Conciliatory.

gre.s: Hoping to end the strike, management adopted a ____ tone, praising the workers' dedication and offering to reopen negotiations.
gre.clue: praising the workers' dedication and offering to reopen negotiations

example: After the heated debate, the club president sent a conciliatory message inviting both factions to discuss the budget over dinner.

en: Intended to teach a lesson, often in a preachy or moralizing way
hook: DIDACTIC: 'DID you get the lesson? ACT on it!' says the preachy teacher.
story: Didactic. Intended to teach a lesson, often in a preachy or moralising way. Every story Russ's grandfather told ended with a moral. The lazy farmer lost his harvest; the honest boy found a gold coin; the greedy cat went hungry. As a child, Russ loved them. As a teenager, he groaned at how didactic they were. Now, raising his own son, he catches himself telling the very same didactic tales, [chuckle] and his son groans too. Didactic comes from the Greek word for teaching. So, what word describes a story that is plainly trying to teach you a moral? ... Didactic.

gre.s: Readers who prefer subtlety may find the novel overly ____, since its author seldom misses a chance to spell out the moral of each chapter.
gre.clue: seldom misses a chance to spell out the moral

example: Children's television in the 1980s was often didactic, with every cartoon ending in a lesson about honesty or brushing one's teeth.

en: To trick or deceive someone; a person who is easily fooled
hook: DUPE: a DOPE who gets fooled.
story: Dupe. To trick or deceive someone; also, a person who is easily fooled. A man phoned Penny's elderly father, claiming to be from his bank, and asked for the code just sent to his phone. He sounded polite and official. Her father was about to read it out when Penny took the phone and hung up. Later they learned the same caller had duped three of their neighbours. Dupe sounds like dope, and a dupe is the person who gets fooled. So, what verb means to trick someone into believing something false? ... Dupe.

gre.s: Investigators believe that a con artist posing as a government official managed to ____ the elderly couple out of their savings.
gre.clue: posing as a government official

example: Fraudsters duped hundreds of job seekers in Dhaka with fake overseas work visas, collecting fees and then vanishing.

en: Having or showing great knowledge gained from study
hook: ERUDITE: 'E-READ-ITE', someone who has read everything.
story: Erudite. Having or showing great knowledge gained from study. Professor Allen's small flat was lined with books from floor to ceiling, in English, Greek, Persian and Sanskrit. When Audrey asked him one question about a medieval poem, he spoke for an hour, quoting from memory, and she filled six pages of notes. She walked home amazed by such an erudite mind. Erudite comes from Latin: e means out of, and rudis means rough, as in rude. Study draws an erudite person out of roughness. So, what word describes someone deeply learned? ... Erudite.

gre.s: Although the lecture was ____, packed with references to obscure philosophers, the speaker made it accessible to a general audience.
gre.clue: packed with references to obscure philosophers

example: My erudite aunt can quote Tagore, Shakespeare, and Rumi in a single conversation, and she remembers exactly where each line comes from.

en: Irrelevant or unnecessary to the subject
hook: EXTRANEOUS: EXTRA, not needed.
story: Extraneous. Irrelevant or unnecessary to the subject. Finn's first GRE essay ran to three pages. It included his views on cricket, a memory of his grandmother, and a line from a film, none of which answered the prompt. His tutor took a red pen and crossed out every extraneous line. What remained was half a page, but it was clear and strong. Extraneous begins with extra: extra material that does not belong. So, what word describes details that have nothing to do with the main point? ... Extraneous.

gre.s: The editor cut several ____ chapters about the author's travels, which had nothing to do with the book's argument about economic policy.
gre.clue: had nothing to do with the book's argument

example: Good photographers crop away extraneous details, so the viewer's eye lands at once on the fisherman's weathered hands.

en: To grow steadily worse when ignored; to become infected and rot
hook: FESTER: like an untreated wound that grows worse.
story: Fester. To grow steadily worse when ignored; to become infected and rot. When Ryan and his brother quarrelled over their father's shop, neither would speak first. Months passed, and the small hurt began to fester. Every family wedding became tense, every holiday lunch silent. Finally their mother sat them down together, and the old anger came out, painful but clean. Fester describes a cut left untreated that swells and rots; a grudge left alone does the same. So, what verb means for a problem or grudge to grow worse when ignored? ... Fester.

gre.s: Left unaddressed, the resentment among the workers continued to ____, eventually erupting in a bitter strike.
gre.clue: eventually erupting in a bitter strike

example: A small quarrel over a borrowed bicycle was allowed to fester for years, until the two cousins no longer spoke at family gatherings.

en: The support on which a lever pivots; a central or essential element
hook: FULCRUM: the PIVOT point of a seesaw.
story: Fulcrum. The support on which a lever pivots; a central or essential element. In a village school, Tommy's science teacher balanced a long bamboo pole across a brick and asked two children to sit at the ends. A small girl lifted a heavy boy simply by sitting farther from the brick. [laugh] The class shrieked with delight. The brick was the fulcrum. "And in a team," the teacher added, "the captain is the fulcrum." The fulcrum is the still point a seesaw turns on. So, what word means the point a lever turns on? ... Fulcrum.

gre.s: As the only member trusted by both factions, the young senator became the ____ of the negotiations, the point around which every compromise turned.
gre.clue: the point around which every compromise turned

example: Physics students laid a ruler across a pencil as a fulcrum and balanced coins at each end to test the law of the lever.

en: Done carelessly, with no clear order, system, or method
hook: HAP-HAZARD: by HAPpenstance and HAZARD, by chance.
story: Haphazard. Done carelessly, with no clear order, system, or method. When Max moved into a new flat, he threw everything into boxes without labels: shoes with spices, books with plates. On the first night he spent an hour searching for his toothbrush and finally found it inside the rice cooker. [sigh] His packing had been completely haphazard. Hap is an old word for chance, as in happen, and a hazard is a risk: haphazard means left to chance. So, what word describes work done with no plan or order? ... Haphazard.

gre.s: Because the samples were collected in a ____ manner, with no consistent procedure, the study's conclusions cannot be trusted.
gre.clue: with no consistent procedure

example: The city's haphazard growth has left whole neighborhoods in Dhaka without parks, footpaths, or room for a fire truck to pass.

en: Seeming real or true but actually false
hook: ILLUSORY: an ILLUSION.
story: Illusory. Seeming real or true but actually false. Driving towards the beach on a hot afternoon, Susie saw what looked like a shining pool of water on the road ahead. Yet however far they drove, it stayed just out of reach. Her father smiled and explained that it was a mirage, a trick of hot air and light. The water was entirely illusory. Illusory is the adjective from illusion: something illusory exists only as an illusion. So, what word describes something that seems real but is not? ... Illusory.

gre.s: The economic boom proved ____: once the speculative bubble burst, it became clear that little real wealth had been created.
gre.clue: little real wealth had been created

example: The sense of safety inside the old building proved illusory when inspectors found deep cracks in every supporting column.

en: Hardworking and diligent
hook: INDUSTRIOUS: works like a whole INDUSTRY.
story: Industrious. Hardworking and diligent. Every morning at five, Joy opens her small tailoring shop. She stitches blouses until noon, teaches two girls to sew in the afternoon, and sits with her son over his homework at night. On Fridays she still finds time to sell homemade pickles to her neighbours. Everyone in the lane calls her the most industrious woman they know. Industrious shares its root with industry: an industrious person works like a whole factory. So, what word describes someone who is always busy and working hard? ... Industrious.

gre.s: Though he had a reputation for laziness as a student, as an apprentice he proved remarkably ____, often staying at the workshop long after everyone else had gone home.
gre.clue: often staying at the workshop long after everyone else had gone home

example: Industrious tailors in Old Dhaka often stitch until midnight in the weeks before Eid, filling orders for an entire neighborhood.

en: Openly rude and insulting, showing no respect at all
hook: INSOLENT: INSULTING.
story: Insolent. Openly rude and insulting, showing no respect at all. When the elderly librarian at Reid's college asked a student to lower his voice, the boy put his feet on the table, looked her in the eye, and laughed in her face. The whole reading room fell silent. Reid felt his face burn with shame. Such insolent behaviour shocked even the boy's own friends. Insolent sounds like insult, and an insolent person insults with every word and look. So, what word describes someone openly and boldly disrespectful? ... Insolent.

gre.s: The new recruit's ____ remarks to the general, delivered with a smirk in front of the entire regiment, earned him a week of confinement to barracks.
gre.clue: delivered with a smirk in front of the entire regiment

example: The insolent customer tossed his money on the counter and snapped his fingers at the pharmacist to hurry up.

en: Clear enough for someone to understand
hook: INTELLIGIBLE: your INTELLIGENCE can grasp it.
story: Intelligible. Clear enough for someone to understand. On a crackling phone line from a far-off village, Lauren's grandmother was trying to tell her something important. Every second word broke into static. Lauren climbed up to the roof, where the signal was stronger, and at last the voice became intelligible: "Bring the green chilli pickle when you come." [laugh] Intelligible shares its root with intelligence, from the Latin for to understand. So, what word describes speech that is clear enough to understand? ... Intelligible.

gre.s: So badly damaged was the recording that the speaker's words were barely ____, and transcribers had to guess at nearly every sentence.
gre.clue: transcribers had to guess at nearly every sentence

example: After weeks of practice, the Danish volunteer's Bangla became intelligible enough for bargaining with vegetable sellers at Karwan Bazar.

en: Tired, slow, and without the energy to do much
hook: LETHARGIC: like LETHE, the river of forgetting and sleep.
story: Lethargic. Tired, slow, and without the energy to do much. After a huge holiday lunch of biryani, creamy curry and three kinds of dessert, Danny's whole family sank into the sofas. Nobody wanted to move. The fan turned slowly overhead, the cousins yawned, and even the cat lay flat on the cool floor. [sigh] The house stayed lethargic until evening tea. Lethargy comes from the Greek lethe, forgetfulness, the name of a mythical river of oblivion: a lethargic person seems to have forgotten how to move. So, what word describes feeling sluggish and drained of energy? ... Lethargic.

gre.s: The usually energetic puppy became ____ after the surgery, sleeping most of the day and showing no interest in its toys.
gre.clue: sleeping most of the day and showing no interest in its toys

example: A heavy lunch of rice and beef curry left the whole office lethargic, and the afternoon meeting crawled along between yawns.

en: Made up of many different parts, sides, or features
hook: MULTI-FACETED: like a diamond with many FACETS.
story: Multifaceted. Made up of many different parts, sides, or features. The great writer Tagore was a poet, but also a songwriter, painter, novelist, playwright, and the founder of a university. Sheryl's teacher held up a glass prism and turned it slowly, so light flashed from every side. "Tagore was like this," she said. "A multifaceted genius." A facet is one flat face of a cut diamond, so multifaceted means having many faces, each shining differently. So, what word describes a person or problem with many different sides? ... Multifaceted.

gre.s: Poverty is a ____ problem, involving not just income but also health, education, and housing, so no single policy can hope to solve it.
gre.clue: involving not just income but also health, education, and housing

example: The multifaceted festival in Sylhet combined poetry readings, folk music, boat races, and a science fair for local schools.

en: Appearing casually calm and relaxed; not showing concern
hook: NON-CHALANT: 'non chaleur' means no heat. Totally cool.
story: Nonchalant. Appearing casually calm and relaxed; not showing concern. In the last over, with six runs needed, Arlo walked out to bat as if strolling to a tea stall. He adjusted his helmet, tapped the pitch, and hit the first ball for four. Everyone else was biting their nails, but he looked completely nonchalant. Only later did he admit his knees had been shaking. Nonchalant comes from French for not caring, from a root that meant to be warm; a nonchalant person never heats up. So, what word describes someone who seems coolly unconcerned? ... Nonchalant.

gre.s: Despite the enormous stakes, the young chess player appeared ____ throughout the final, chatting casually with spectators between moves.
gre.clue: chatting casually with spectators between moves

example: The rickshaw puller stayed nonchalant as buses roared past within inches, steering calmly through the evening rush on Elephant Road.

en: Extremely unpleasant; hateful
hook: ODIOUS: full of ODOR and hatred.
story: Odious. Extremely unpleasant; hateful. A city landlord raised the rent in the middle of the rainy season and threatened to throw out a family whose child was sick. The neighbours were disgusted. Even his own nephew called the act odious and moved out in protest. Some behaviour is so cruel that people cannot bear to look at it. Odious comes from the Latin odium, hatred, and we still say a cruel act brings odium on the person who does it. So, what word describes conduct that deserves to be hated? ... Odious.

gre.s: Though the essayist praised the dictator's economic reforms, she found his persecution of journalists so ____ that she refused to attend any event held in his honor.
gre.clue: refused to attend any event held in his honor

example: Most voters found the candidate's odious jokes about disabled people impossible to forgive, and his support collapsed within a week.

en: Present everywhere at the same time
hook: OMNI = all, PRESENT = there. Present everywhere.
story: Omnipresent. Present everywhere at the same time. During the football World Cup, the whole country turns into a sea of flags. On the rooftops of the old city, the flags of Argentina and Brazil flutter side by side, and they hang from rickshaws, tea stalls and the backs of buses. On his way to school, Bobby counted forty of them. For a month, they are omnipresent. Omni means all, as in omnivore, an animal that eats everything; omnipresent means present in all places. So, what word describes something you see absolutely everywhere? ... Omnipresent.

gre.s: In the city's busiest district, security cameras are virtually ____, mounted on nearly every corner and doorway.
gre.clue: mounted on nearly every corner and doorway

example: During the monsoon in Dhaka, the smell of wet earth and frying jilapi seems omnipresent, drifting through every lane and bus window.

en: A solution or remedy for all problems
hook: PAN-ACEA: PAN = all. A cure for ALL.
story: Panacea. A solution or remedy for all problems. In many family homes, someone treats a single remedy as a panacea. Sheila's aunt believes black seed oil can cure coughs, back pain, hair loss, and even exam nerves. Sheila loves her for it, but she knows no medicine is a true panacea. Real problems usually need different solutions. Pan means all, as in pandemic, and akos means cure in Greek: a panacea is a cure for all. So, what word means a single remedy for every problem? ... Panacea.

gre.s: Although technology can help, experts caution that it is no ____ for the deep social problems that affect the nation's schools.
gre.clue: the deep social problems

example: Some parents treat extra coaching centers as a panacea for poor grades, though a tired child rarely learns more after ten hours of study.

en: Just good enough; adequate
hook: PASSABLE: good enough to PASS, but no more.
story: Passable. Just good enough; adequate. Megan cooked her first chicken curry for her in-laws, as nervous as an exam candidate. It was too salty in places and the potatoes were hard, but nobody went hungry. Her father-in-law tasted it, chewed slowly, [chuckle] and declared it passable. Megan took that as high praise, and a year later her curry was the best in the family. Passable means good enough to pass, like a mark that clears the line and no more. So, what word describes something adequate but not impressive? ... Passable.

gre.s: Although his English was merely ____, sufficient for ordering meals and asking directions, it was hardly fluent enough for him to follow the technical lectures.
gre.clue: sufficient for ordering meals and asking directions

example: Ruma's first attempt at baking bread was passable, a little dense in the middle but good enough to eat with butter and tea.

en: To calm someone's anger by doing something to please them
hook: PLACATE: give a PLATE of food to calm someone down.
story: Placate. To calm someone's anger by doing something to please them. Tanya's little brother screamed in the middle of the supermarket because she refused to buy him chocolate. People turned to stare. [sigh] Desperate, she offered him a ride in the trolley, and he was instantly placated. Later their mother [laugh] shook her head. "You placated him this time, but now he knows the trick." Placate is related to placid, meaning calm: to placate someone is to make them placid again. So, what verb means to soothe an angry person by giving them something? ... Placate.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious shareholders, the board announced a generous dividend just days after the scandal broke.
gre.clue: furious shareholders

example: To placate the neighbors who complained about the noise, the band offered them free tickets to its next concert at the community hall.

en: Done suddenly without careful thought (adj.); to cause something to happen suddenly (verb)
hook: PRECIPITATE: like rain falling suddenly from the sky (precipitation).
story: Precipitate. As an adjective, done suddenly without careful thought. As a verb, to make something happen suddenly. Angry after one argument with his manager, Spencer typed his resignation and sent it within ten minutes. By evening he regretted the precipitate decision. Worse, his email precipitated a crisis, because two colleagues quit with him. Precipitate comes from the Latin for headlong, falling headfirst, the same root that gives us precipice, a steep cliff. So, what word describes a decision made suddenly, without thinking it through? ... Precipitate.

gre.s: Investors feared that the bank's ____ sale of its assets, announced without any consultation, would trigger a broader panic.
gre.clue: announced without any consultation

example: Their precipitate decision to marry after only two weeks surprised both families, though the couple is still happy decades later.

en: Conformity to accepted standards of behavior or morals
hook: PROPRIETY: PROPER behavior.
story: Propriety. Conformity to accepted standards of behaviour or morals. At her grandfather's funeral prayers, Rhoda noticed her young cousin chatting loudly on his phone in the courtyard. An uncle quietly took the phone and reminded him of propriety: this was a time for silence and respect. The boy lowered his eyes and stood with the others. Propriety comes from proper, meaning proper behaviour; do not confuse it with property. So, what word means correct, respectable conduct that a situation demands? ... Propriety.

gre.s: The minister resigned not because he had broken the law but because his conduct raised serious questions of ____.
gre.clue: not because he had broken the law

example: Out of propriety, the young lecturer refused to grade his cousin's exam paper and asked a colleague to mark it instead.

en: To forcefully stop or suppress; to officially reject
hook: QUASH: SQUASH it flat.
story: Quash. To forcefully stop or suppress; to officially reject. A rumour spread through Simon's college group chats that the final exams had been cancelled. Within hours, hundreds of students had stopped studying. Then the principal posted a short notice: the exams would go ahead as planned. With a single line, he quashed the rumour. Courts, too, can quash a verdict, cancelling it officially. Quash sounds like squash: you squash a bug flat, and you quash a rumour flat. So, what verb means to crush a rumour or overturn a decision? ... Quash.

gre.s: The regime moved swiftly to ____ the rebellion, arresting its leaders and banning public gatherings before the unrest could spread to other cities.
gre.clue: before the unrest could spread to other cities

example: The High Court quashed the lower court's verdict after new evidence showed that the main witness had been bribed.

en: Skilled at gaining advantage through cunning
hook: WILY: like WILE E. Coyote, always scheming.
story: Wily. Skilled at gaining advantage through cunning. In old folktales the jackal is always the clever one, and one wily old jackal kept raiding Uncle Ray's chicken coop. Fences, traps and a sleeping dog all failed; the jackal seemed to know every plan in advance. One night it slipped through a gap no wider than a hand and took the fattest hen. [chuckle] Even Uncle Ray admired it a little. A wile is a clever trick, so a wily creature is full of wiles. So, what word describes someone cunning and full of tricks? ... Wily.

gre.s: The ____ negotiator let her opponents believe they had won every minor point, all the while maneuvering toward the one concession she actually wanted.
gre.clue: all the while maneuvering toward

example: The wily old shopkeeper always displayed his best mangoes on top of the basket and hid the bruised ones underneath.
